case_name: Royal Bank of Canada v. B.M.P. Global Distribution Inc.
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Royal Bank of Canada v. B.M.P.
Global Distribution Inc.,

2007 BCSC 1438

Date: 20070927

Docket:
S023327

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Royal Bank of Canada

Plaintiff

And

B.M.P. Global Distribution Inc.,

636651 B.C. Ltd., Audie Hashka and
Paul Backman

Defendants

Before:
The Honourable Madam Justice Ross

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff

D.
Ross McGowan

Robert Dawkins

Counsel for the Defendants

Paul
E. Jaffe

Counsel for
Proposed Defendant Debra Backman

Dean
T. Fox

Date and Place of Trial/Hearing:

August
7-10

Vancouver,
B.C.

Introduction

[
1
]

This is an application by the defendants B.M.P.
Global Distribution Inc., 636651 B.C. Ltd., Audie Hashka and Paul Backman, brought
pursuant to rules 18(6) and 19(24) for an order striking the amended statement
of claim.

[
2
]

In the present action the plaintiff, Royal Bank
of Canada (“RBC”), seeks to recover loss and damages arising out of the
negotiation of a counterfeit cheque to the defendant B.M.P. Global Distribution
Inc. (“BMP”) and what RBC describes as the defendants’ subsequent efforts to
obtain a windfall in the proceeds obtained from negotiation of the cheque,
despite what RBC claims is its clearly superior claim to the proceeds.

[
3
]

The circumstances surrounding this counterfeit
cheque and its subsequent negotiation have given rise to two lawsuits.  The
first action was a suit by the defendants in this action, as plaintiffs, against
their own bank, the Bank of Nova Scotia (the “BNS Action”) for,
inter alia
,
breach of contract.  The Bank of Nova Scotia had, at the request of RBC, frozen
funds in the plaintiffs’ accounts and then transferred funds representing some
of the proceeds of the counterfeit cheque back to RBC.  The plaintiffs asserted
that this conduct was in breach of the Bank’s obligations to its customers.  RBC
was not a party to the BNS Action.  The BNS Action proceeded to a summary
trial, the results of which were set aside by the Court of Appeal, and then to a
full trial and subsequent appeal.

[
4
]

The present lawsuit was commenced during the
course of the BNS Action but, in circumstances discussed more fully below, was
held in abeyance while the BNS Action proceeded.  The essence of this
application brought by the defendants is that the claim of RBC discloses no cause
of action, is unnecessary, vexatious, an abuse of process and a collateral
attack on the judgment in the BNS Action, and for those reasons, the action
must be dismissed.

Facts

Circumstances Surrounding the
Cheque

[
5
]

The essential facts giving rise to the
litigation are set out in the judgment of Mr. Justice Cohen in
B.M.P
Global Distribution Inc. v. Bank of Nova Scotia
,
2005 BCSC 1091
, 8
B.L.R. (4th) 247 [
BNS Trial Decision
].  The following description
of the events is adopted from Cohen J.’s findings.

[
6
]

Paul Backman and Audie Hashka are the directors
of BMP.  636651 B.C. Ltd. ("636651") is Mr. Hashka's holding company.
In 2001, each of the companies had a corporate account at the Bank of Nova
Scotia.  Mr. Backman and Mr. Hashka also had personal accounts at the Bank
of Nova Scotia.  Mr. Backman's two accounts were held jointly with his wife.

[
7
]

BMP was incorporated in July 1999.  It is in the
business of distributing non-stick bakeware manufactured and supplied by Pantec
Technologies (“Pantec”).  BMP acts as Pantec’s commercial distributor, but
without any written distribution agreement granting BMP distribution rights.
BMP does not own any interest in the line of bakeware manufactured by Pantec.

[
8
]

Mr. Backman and Mr. Hashka testified that between
August and September 2001, they reached an agreement with Mr. Sunn Newman of Sunrise
Marketing, whereby BMP agreed to sell the right to distribute the bakeware in a
portion of the United States to Mr. Newman for $1.2 million USD.  The
circumstances described by Mr. Backman and Mr. Hashka were somewhat unusual for
a commercial transaction of this magnitude.  Cohen J. summarized these circumstances
at paras 12-16:

Hashka described the negotiations with Newman
as follows:

I come up with the
number, "How does $1.2 million US sound," when we're looking at, you
know, what was in the east that still was, you know, possible clientele.
There's large bake
—
larger franchises, like Krogers,
—
you know, things like
that. And so I came up with the number 1.2 million US. I called [Mr. Newman]
back. I think I caught a hold of him in Houston and put the number onto him. He
said, "Okay. I'll confer with my partners on what they think." I said
"Fine. If you're interested that's the number we're looking at. You get
back to me." And that's how I left it with him.

Backman agreed that Hashka arrived at the price
of USD $1.2 million by pulling the number out of the air. BMP Global had no
projected cash flow statements, business plans or marketing plans that were
used as the basis for the negotiations. Further, Newman did not request copies
of BMP Global's financial statements or sales records (indicating a net loss of
approximately $3,500), nor did BMP Global offer to provide this kind of
information to Newman.

Backman and Hashka did no research into Newman
or Sunrise Marketing. They did not ask Newman for financial statements, nor did
they request information on Newman's previous experience in the distribution
business.

The plaintiffs’ knowledge of Newman was
described by Backman, as follows:

Q.        Okay.  So what did
—
what did you know about
Sunrise Marketing?

A.        Just that it was Mr. Newman who we were doing business
with.

Q.        And what
did you know about Mr. Newman?

A.        Only that he was a sharp-looking guy that seemed like he
had a lot of potential.

Hashka said:

Q.        [C]an you give us a sense of what you knew
about Newman or what your feeling was about him in your dealings with him?

A.        Well, he seemed like a professional. He
dressed well. He seemed professional. He seemed like a businessman to me.

[
9
]

On October 22, 2001, BMP received a cheque for
$904,563.00 (the “Cheque”).  The Cheque was on a customized cheque form from
First National Financial Corporation (“First National”), written on an account
at the Royal Bank of Canada and purporting to be signed by two signatories.  The
Cheque came by courier with no covering letter.  It contained no indication of
its purpose.  The contact information on the envelope was E. Smith.  Neither
the drawer of the Cheque nor E. Smith were known to Mr. Backman or Mr. Haska.
They made no attempt to contact either First National or E. Smith at the
address or telephone number listed on the courier envelope.

[
10
]

Cohen J. found that the Cheque was counterfeit
and that the plaintiffs gave no consideration to anyone for its receipt.

[
11
]

On October 22, 2001, Mr. Hashka and Mr.
Backman took the Cheque to their branch of the Bank of Nova Scotia and spoke to
the Branch Manager, Jeff Richards, who had known the men since 1998.  Mr.
Hashka told Mr. Richards the Cheque was a down payment for distributor rights
for their product.

[
12
]

At the time the Cheque was presented for
deposit, the balance in the BMP account was $59.67.  Mr. Backman and Mr. Hashka
were not given immediate access to the funds.  A hold was placed on the funds
because BMP did not have sufficient funds in its account to cover the amount in
the event that the Cheque was returned.

[
13
]

Mr. Richards asked his Service Manager to phone
RBC to take steps to verify the Cheque.  Mr. Richards was told funds were
available and there was no stop payment on the Cheque.  Mr. Richards instructed
his staff to fax a copy of the cheque to RBC.

[
14
]

In the days that followed, Mr. Hashka and Mr. Backman
had discussions with Mr. Richards about some of the unusual circumstances
surrounding the C
heque.  Mr. Hashka informed Mr. Richards that
BMP’s customer on the distribution deal was Summit Marketing and that they were
dealing with a Mr. Danko.  They did not refer to Sunrise Marketing or Mr.
Newman.

[
15
]

The Cheque was cleared through the clearing
system and on October 30, 2001, Mr. Haska and Mr. Backman were allowed to deal
with the funds.

Over the next ten days a
number of payments were made from the BMP account.  There were a series of
payments to the accounts of Mr. Backman, Mr. Hashka and 636651.  A number of
payments were made to third parties.  Mr. Justice Cohen stated at para. 28-31:

When the seven day hold was released Hashka and
Backman were allowed to deal with the Funds.  On October 30, 2001, and
over the next ten days, BMP Global made numerous payments from the BMP Account,
including a number of payments to Hashka, Backman and 636651.

With the exception of a payment of $3,000 to
Raynier on October 30, 2001, all payments from the BMP Account to parties other
than the plaintiffs between October 30, 2001 and November 9, 2001 were related
to the payment of pre-existing debts incurred before their receipt of the
Counterfeit Cheque.  These debts existed entirely independently of the
receipt by BMP Global of the Counterfeit Cheque and were not incurred in reliance
on receipt of the Counterfeit Cheque.

On November 7, 2001, Hashka requested the BNS
to transfer USD $20,000 to an account at the Citibank in New York City payable
to LMB Prestsquare, Advice A.U. Salamain.  Both Hashka and Backman
testified that they do not know LMB Prestsquare or A.U. Salamain. The wire
transfer was processed on November 8, 2001, resulting in a debit to the BMP
Account of $32,157.

The other payments
out of the BMP Account between October 30, 2001 and November 9, 2001, totalling
approximately $790,000 related to the transfer of the Funds by BMP Global to
other accounts operated by the plaintiffs.  No financial statements or
other documents have been produced to explain the basis upon which the Funds
were distributed to the plaintiffs.  The Funds were either disbursed by
the plaintiffs, returned to the BMP Account or remained to the credit of the
plaintiffs’ various accounts on November 9, 2001.

[
16
]

On November 9, 2001, Mr. Richards received a
telephone call from a person at RBC advising him that the Cheque had not been
issued by First National.
Later that day, he contacted Mr.
Backman and Mr. Hashka and informed them of the situation.

[
17
]

Mr. Richards also contacted Ray Scheller, the
Regional Manager for Investigation and Loss Prevention for the Bank of Nova
Scotia in Vancouver.  Mr. Scheller took steps to issue a grid warning with
respect to the Cheque.  Cohen J. described grid warnings at para. 48:

A grid warning is
a form of communication between financial institutions by which they, through
their corporate security departments, seek assistance and share information.
In November 2001, all grid warnings in the Lower Mainland were issued by
the corporate security office of the Bank of Montreal.  This was done by
agreement between the financial institutions to ensure consistency and
uniformity in the grid warnings that were issued.  Distribution of grid
warnings is limited to corporate security offices of financial institutions in
the Lower Mainland.  On average, five to six grid warnings are issued each
day.

[
18
]

The Bank of Nova Scotia then froze the accounts
of BMP, 636651, Mr. Hashka and Mr. Backman.  The Bank of Nova Scotia ultimately
entered into an agreement with RBC whereby, at RBC’s request, the Bank of Nova
Scotia agreed to restrain and remit to RBC the frozen funds and RBC agreed to
indemnify the Bank of Nova Scotia.  The frozen funds were made up as follows:

Account

Amount

BMP Account

$ 350,188.65

636651 Account

$ 393,000.00

Backman Chequing Account

$  17,711.17

Hashka Account

$  13,104.87

Backman Savings Account

$   2, 645.79

TOTAL

$ 776,650.48

[
19
]

In addition to the amounts frozen, the Bank of
Nova Scotia recovered $685.56 by reversing certain bill payments that had been
made by BMP.  The total amount frozen or recovered was $777,336.04 (the
“Recovered Funds”).  The difference between the funds advanced on the basis of
the Cheque, $904,563.00 (the “Funds”), and the Recovered Funds, is $127,226.96 (the
“Outstanding Amount”).

[
20
]

As of the date of the trial, Cohen J. noted that
Mr. Hashka and Mr. Backman had not been able to contact Mr. Newman.  Mr. Newman
had not contacted them, either with respect to the Cheque or the alleged
distribution agreement.  The plaintiffs had not commenced proceedings against
Mr. Newman or Sunrise Marketing to enforce the alleged agreement.

The Litigation

[
21
]

The BNS Action was commenced by writ of summons
dated December 21, 2001.  The plaintiffs were BMP, 636651 B.C. Ltd., Audie
Hashka and Paul Backman.  The defendants were the Bank of Nova Scotia doing business
as Scotiabank and the said Scotiabank (“BNS”).  The claim was for damages for
libel and slander arising from matters in relation to the grid warnings, breach
of contract, negligence, conversion, money had and received, breach of
fiduciary duty, and breaches of the
Privacy Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c.
P-21 and
Bills of Exchange Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-4.  The
plaintiffs in the BNS Action initially sought,
inter alia
, release of what
were described as the frozen funds, which were in effect the Recovered Funds as
those funds had in fact been transferred to RBC, damages including punitive
damages and a declaration that the plaintiffs owned the funds that BNS had
frozen.

[
22
]

BNS filed a statement of defence dated January
23, 2002.  It pleaded, in addition to a general denial of the plaintiffs’
claims, that the Cheque was a counterfeit and not a genuine cheque drawn by
First National, and that BNS transferred the Recovered Funds to RBC on the
basis that the Cheque had been credited to the BMP account by BNS acting under
a mistake of fact.  BNS sought to have the action dismissed.

[
23
]

In April 2002, the plaintiffs in the BNS Action set
the matter down for summary trial pursuant to rule 18A.  The matter was to be
heard on June 24 and 25, 2002.  The relief sought was an order for damages, or
return of the Recovered Funds.  The plaintiffs did not seek a declaration of
ownership of the Recovered Funds.

[
24
]

By writ and statement of claim dated June 12,
2002, RBC commenced the present action (the “RBC Action”) in which RBC is the
plaintiff and the BMP parties (the plaintiffs in the BNS Action) are the
defendants.  The action concerned the Funds, which were defined as the amount
credited by BNS to the BMP account in relation to the Cheque.  RBC pleaded that
the Cheque was counterfeit and that because the Cheque had cleared the clearing
system, BNS had received payment for the amount of the Cheque from RBC.  It
pleaded that as a consequence, RBC was defrauded through the creation of the
Cheque.  RBC pleaded that at all times, all right, title, interest or property
in the Funds remained with it and that at no time did the defendants acquire
any interest in the Funds or were the defendants entitled to the Funds.  RBC
sought a declaration that it was entitled to trace the Recovered Funds and an
order that the defendants were liable to it for the Outstanding Amount.

[
25
]

BNS filed a response in relation to the motion
for a summary trial in the BNS Action in which it took the position that the
matter was inappropriate for determination by way of rule 18A.  BNS noted that
RBC had commenced an action seeking a declaration that it was entitled to the
return of the Funds advanced on the basis of the counterfeit Cheque and seeking
an order requiring the defendants to repay the outstanding amount.  BNS stated
that the two actions should proceed together as they raise the same issues.

[
26
]

A statement of defence in the RBC Action was
filed dated July 30, 2002.  The defendants denied that the Cheque was
counterfeit and pleaded, in the alternative, that RBC was negligent and in
breach of its duty to take steps to ensure that the Cheque was genuine.  They
pleaded that all transactions conducted by the defendants were undertaken in
reliance upon RBC’s representation that the Cheque was genuine and with the
belief that their right to spend the funds was unfettered.

[
27
]

Shortly before the rule 18A application was
scheduled to proceed in the BNS Action, BNS filed an amended statement of
defence dated August 22, 2002.  In it, BNS made reference to the suspicious
circumstances surrounding the delivery of the Cheque and pleaded that the plaintiffs
failed to disclose the suspicious circumstances to BNS.  BNS also pleaded that at
all material times, the amount credited to the BMP account was the property of
First National, who requested its return through RBC.

[
28
]

The reasons for the summary trial application were
given by Madam Justice Humphries in
B.M.P. Global v. Scotiabank
,

2002 BCSC 1508
, 8 B.C.L.R. (4th) 184, [
BNS 18A
].  It was clear
that Madam Justice Humphries was aware of the RBC Action.  She noted at paras.
12-13:

On December 21, 2001, the plaintiffs sued
Scotiabank for return of the money and for consequential damages for the way in
which Scotiabank dealt with them and allegedly damaged their business
reputation (the latter claim not being part of this application); Royal Bank
has now initiated a separate action against the plaintiffs, I presume for the
balance of the money. That action is not before me.

The Statement of
Claim sounds in breach of contract, libel, slander, negligence, conversion,
money had and received, breach of fiduciary duty, breach of the
Privacy
Act
and breach of the
Bills of Exchange Act
, but the
argument before me centered on contract. The Statement of Defence as originally
filed pleaded only mistake of fact. It has now been amended to include a
defence of lawful justification in respect of the crediting of the Royal Bank
with the funds, and breach of various obligations on the part of the
plaintiffs. In neither version has fraud or any involvement in the production of
the cheque on the part of the plaintiffs been alleged.

[
29
]

The plaintiffs were seeking resolution of a
limited question in the 18A application in the BNS Action.  Humphries J.
described the plaintiffs’ position as follows at paras. 19-20:

Although there are remedies sought in equity in
the Statement of Claim, the plaintiffs did not pursue them at trial,
concentrating on their claim of debt under the Financial Services Agreement
("the contract"), which is a standard banking contract of adhesion.

The plaintiffs'
position is simple: they maintain that, settlement having been received, the
bank had no authority to charge their account.
Whatever the rights of the
Royal Bank, and whoever is eventually entitled to the money
, Scotiabank
could not simply take the money from their accounts and send it off to the
Royal Bank. By doing so Scotiabank breached its contract with the plaintiff and
is in debt to the plaintiffs for the amounts taken from their account.
[emphasis added]

[
30
]

Madam Justice Humphries concluded that it was
appropriate to deal with the “very narrow” issue that was before her; namely,
could the bank transfer the funds in the plaintiffs’ account to RBC.  She
stated her conclusions with respect to this issue at paras. 35-38:

It may be that the plaintiffs have suffered
consequential damage through the manner in which the defendants dealt with
their accounts; that issue is not before me and will go to the trial list.
However, the plaintiffs have suffered no damage by having the money, which was
never real and never theirs, taken from their accounts. To ignore the fact that
there was no underlying transaction through which the plaintiffs had any valid
or legally enforceable expectation of money, were owed any money, or were put
at risk by not receiving the money, would indeed be to sanction a windfall,
created through "legal legerdemain”.

In the result, I find that the bank did breach
the contract when it transferred the funds out of the plaintiffs' account to
the Royal Bank, but the plaintiff did not suffer a loss by the transfer of
those funds, other than whatever consequential damages might be proven at
trial. That issue is referred to the trial list. Although I am not seized, I
will hear it if counsel can arrange a convenient time through the registry.

There are other considerations and other
arguments to be made in respect of entitlement to the money which is the
subject of the action by the Royal Bank; that action is not based upon the
contract in issue here. As well, there may be different evidence before the court
on that action. Obviously, I can make no finding in this action which is
relevant to the sorts of losses or claims that may or may not have occurred in
that context.

The plaintiff has
succeeded in proving a breach, but the defendant has succeeded in their
position that there has been no loss.

[
31
]

The plaintiffs appealed and BNS cross-appealed.
The plaintiffs took the position at the appeal that “this is simply a question
of breach of contract and that that issue proceeds on undisputed facts.”  The
Court of Appeal, in
B.M.P. Global et al. v. Bank of Nova Scotia
,

2003 BCCA 534
, 19 B.C.L.R. (4th) 347, concluded that the issue should not have
been decided pursuant to rule 18A, set aside the order and remitted the matter
to trial.

[
32
]

The reasons of the Court of Appeal were
pronounced on September 30, 2003.  The BNS Action was at that point set down
for trial commencing January 12, 2004.  By letter dated October 10, 2003, Douglas
G.S. Rae, Q.C., counsel for both BNS and RBC, wrote to Paul E. Jaffe, counsel
for the plaintiffs in the BNS Action, and to Dean T. Fox, counsel for the
defendants in the RBC Action.  The letter sought consent to an order that the
BNS and RBC Actions be heard together.  Mr. Rae stated:

Our clients wish the BNS Action and the RBC
Action to be heard together.  The two actions arise from the same facts and
involve common questions of both law and fact. On this basis, it is our
position that it is desirable to dispose of both actions at the same time.
Proceeding in this manner will save time and expense and will be more
convenient for all parties and the court.

Related to the
issue of the hearing of the two actions together, is the matter of discovery
evidence.  We suggest that the parties agree that the examinations for
discovery and exchange of documents that has taken place to date be available
for use by the parties in both actions.  This will ensure that both matters can
proceed to trial on the scheduled trial date and will save the parties the time
and expense of conducting further discoveries that would be largely duplicative
of the discoveries which have already occurred.  We have previously raised this
issue for your consideration in respect of documents in our correspondence to
Mr. Fox (copied to Mr. Jaffe) dated January 28, 2003 and March 5, 2003.

[
33
]

Mr. Jaffe responded by letter of the same date.
He was opposed to having the matters heard together, in part because of a
concern that the effect of such an order would be to compromise the trial
date.  Mr. Jaffe stated in part:

The essence of the counterclaim as yet to be
filed in the RBC action is that RBC induced Scotiabank to breach its contracts
with my clients. That decision, we say, was based on legal advice received by
RBC between November 16, 2001 and December 6, 2001, leading to an agreement
between the banks to circumvent the court regarding transfer of the subject
funds. It is my clients’ intention to proceed with that trial via a jury.

The above counterclaim is unnecessary and
potentially embarrassing if, at the Scotiabank trial, the court finds
Scotiabank’s actions to not be in breath of contract. Ideally, such
counterclaim which may intrude upon the dealings between the banks and their
counsel should not be launched until such time as the contract issues with
Scotiabank have been adjudicated. I trust you agree that this is a responsible
approach to take.

In addition, as earlier communicated (eg. see
my letters to Jennifer Francis), given the restrictions upon a party’s use of
documents and information generated through discovery in the Scotiabank case
(along with Scotiabank’s common law and contractual duties to safeguard the
privacy of my clients’ banking, personal and business affairs), your law firm
remains precluded from disclosing such confidential information to RBC.

In my respectful
view, I believe your law firm is in a disqualifying conflict if both actions
are to proceed together. However, until now, the RBC action has been held in
abeyance pending the outcome of the Scotiabank case. This was a course all
parties accepted in order that my clients’ claim against Scotiabank can be
dealt with. If the RBC action is now to be activated, and if your firm now
intends to proceed with discoveries of my clients in that action, your law
firm’s dual role in this matter is unacceptable to my clients.

[
34
]

In the result, no application to have the two
actions heard together was brought and the BNS Action proceeded to trial before
Cohen J.  On November 3, 2003, the plaintiffs filed an amended statement of
claim in the BNS Action.  Included in the amendment was a change to paragraph
18.  The original pleading stated:

As a result of the
Defendant’s conduct herein the Plaintiffs have suffered damages including loss
of funds belonging to the Plaintiffs, losses arising from the Defendants
interference with the Plaintiffs’ businesses and damage to the reputation of
each of the Plaintiffs.

The amended paragraph now reads:

As a result of the
Defendant’s conduct herein the Plaintiffs have suffered damages including
loss
of credit in their respective bank accounts
, // losses arising from the
Defendants interference with the Plaintiffs’ businesses and damage to the
reputation of each of the Plaintiffs.  [emphasis in original]

[
35
]

In addition, in the amended statement of claim, the
declaration with respect to ownership of the funds was deleted from the prayer
for relief.

[
36
]

Mr. Justice Cohen concluded that BNS had acted
in breach of its contract with the plaintiffs and in breach of the law which
governs banker/customer relations.  At para. 306 of his reasons, he stated:

Thus, I find that
by October 30, 2001, final settlement on the deposit of the Counterfeit Cheque
had been reached between the BNS and the RBC within the meaning of the terms of
the Agreement.  Therefore, the RBC lost recourse against the BNS.  The
Funds went from being a “provisional” credit to being a “final” credit.
At that stage the relationship between the BNS and the plaintiffs was that of
debtor/creditor.  The law provides that a bank may not pay out of a
customer’s account when it does not have permission to do so:  See
Clansmen
Resources Ltd.,

supra,

White,
supra.
Accordingly,
when the BNS froze, retained and later remitted the Recovered Amount to the RBC
without the plaintiff’s permission, it acted in breach of its contractual
obligations to the plaintiffs and contrary to the law which governs
banker/customer relations.

[
37
]

Cohen J. held that the plaintiffs were entitled
to recover damages equal to the Recovered Funds, a $13.50 late charge payable
to Mr. Backman, $7,500.00 for wrongful disclosure of information and defamation,
and court order interest.  He declined to make an award of punitive damages.

[
38
]

BNS appealed and the plaintiffs crossed-appealed
on the issue of punitive damages.  BNS filed a notice of motion seeking a stay
of execution.  BNS reached an agreement with the plaintiffs to resolve the stay
of execution issue, which was documented in a letter dated November 10, 2005.
The terms were as follows:

1.         BNS
will make payment within a reasonable time of $80,000.00 to Paul Jaffe in
trust;

2.         the
payment shall be credited to BNS in the following order until the funds are
exhausted:

(a)       against the heads of damages awarded which are not
appealed from;

(b)       against the costs awarded
at trial; and

(c)        against the outstanding damages should BNS not succeed on
appeal;

3.         execution
on the judgment in the captioned matter, including the order for costs, will be
stayed by consent until final disposition of the appeal;

4.         post
judgment interest shall continue to accrue on unsatisfied amounts ultimately
found to be owing by BNS to the plaintiffs, if any;

5.         the
plaintiffs agree jointly and severally, to repay the part of the payment from
BNS to which the plaintiffs are ultimately found not to be entitled, if any;

6.         counsel for
BNS will file a
Praecipe
adjourning, generally, by consent, the
application set for November 16, 2006.

[
39
]

The reasons of the Court of Appeal in the BNS
Action were given in
B.M.P. Global
Distribution Inc. v. Bank of Nova
Scotia (c.o.b. Scotiabank)
,
2007 BCCA 52
, 63 B.C.L.R. (4th) 214 [
BNS
Appeal
].  The court was clearly alive to the existence of the RBC
Action.  At para. 31 of the reasons Madam Justice Saunders, for the court, wrote:

To unravel the
issue one must first recognize that the case has come to court in an unorthodox
fashion. While in the usual course, a case of a credit generated by a
fraudulent instrument is likely to be commenced by the bank that is out of
pocket, (here the Royal Bank of Canada), seeking restitution on the basis of
mistake of fact, in this case that bank recovered its monies through the
actions of BMP's bank, the Bank of Nova Scotia. Instead the plaintiff here is
BMP, the customer, suing a bank that did not itself have a loss. There is a
separate action commenced by the Royal Bank of Canada against the respondents,
seeking to recover the funds attributable to the counterfeit cheque. The Bank
of Nova Scotia and the Royal Bank of Canada proposed that the actions be heard
together, but that proposal did not prevail. Although not all the parties to
the events were before the court in this case, the case still requires an
examination of the asset that BMP claims was wrongly appropriated from it, in
order that one may know whether it was capable of bearing the value placed upon
it by the damage award.

[
40
]

The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal with
respect to BMP, substituting an order for damages in the amount of $101.00,
representing nominal damages for breach of contract and $100.00 that was not
attributable to the Cheque.  The Court of Appeal based its conclusion on the application
of equitable principles, concluding at para. 44 that:

In my view,
conscience did not give BMP a claim to windfall money derived from the
counterfeit cheque. One may say that the plaintiff BMP lost nothing because it
had nothing in the account - all that was there was a credit created by BMP's
unwitting deposit of a fraudulent instrument.

[
41
]

The appeal with respect to the transfers to
other accounts of the respondents was dismissed for the following reasons given
at paras. 53-56:

The respondents say that the Bank of Nova
Scotia breached their banking contracts by tracing, and debiting, sums
originating with the counterfeit cheque. They say that the Bank forgot their
separate identities in its zeal to prevent dissipation of the credits created
by the counterfeit cheque.

In the case of these respondents, some of the
"funds" were transferred from BMP's account to the others' accounts,
and some were by cheque given by BMP and deposited in their separate accounts.

As to the amounts that derived from cheques issued
by BMP, these cheques, unlike the counterfeit cheque, held the character of
bills of exchange. They did not have the frailty, for example, which engages
s.
48
of the
Bills of Exchange Act
. As against BMP, those cheques
were effective in the absence of fraud. Although the trial judge did not find
the reason that the transfers or cheques were made by BMP, he also did not find
fraud or bad faith in their creation.

In my view, these
cheques and transfers bear a character quite different from the counterfeit
cheque and different from BMP's transfer to and from its own account at the
Bank of Montreal. Absent a finding that they were improperly created, I do not
consider that the Bank of Nova Scotia was entitled to debit these accounts in
these circumstances, as it did. Any remedy here lies as a remedy of tracing, or
an enquiry into the true ownership of the accounts as contemplated in
Bhogal
,

supra
. Those remedies must be pursued through the proper channels and
not, as here, by self-help.

Rule 19(24)

[
42
]

Rule 19(24) provides:

(24)     At any stage of a proceeding the court
may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement,
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)       it discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case may
be,

(b)       it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)        it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or
hearing or the proceeding, or

(d)       it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may
grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order
the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

19(24)(a) No Reasonable Claim

[
43
]

RBC submits that it is the victim, indeed the
only victim, of a fraudulent scheme involving the counterfeit Cheque.  It
submits that it has a superior moral and equitable right to property and funds
traceable to the defendants’ participation in the fraudulent scheme (the
“Disputed Property”), whether it be the Funds, the cause of action of the BMP
parties against BNS, the judgment held by the BMP parties against BNS, or any
other assets.  RBC asserts that the amended statement of claim pleads facts
necessary to support a cause of action for damages, equitable relief for breach
of trust, knowing receipt and to assert a proprietary and tracing claim with
respect to the Disputed Property.

[
44
]

The defendants submit that the pleadings do not
disclose a cause of action because RBC’s own misconduct and delay should
preclude it from equitable relief and because the loss arises, not from the
counterfeit Cheque, but from the indemnity agreement with BNS.  The defendants
submit that whatever enrichment of the defendants has taken place is by reason
of a juristic reason, that is, their judgments against BNS, and RBC has no
corresponding deprivation as whatever amount RBC may pay under the Indemnity
Agreement, it is going to BNS, not the defendants and is not the cause of the
“enrichment” of the defendants.

[
45
]

The defendants further submit that if RBC
decided to indemnify BNS, that was RBC’s decision. However, it did so voluntarily
as BNS was in no position to have the agreement enforced by the court. The defendants
rely upon G.H.L. Fridman & James G. McLeod,
Restitution
(Toronto:
The Carswell Company Ltd.,
1982) at 294:

The reasons for this attitude of the law
relate to the public interest, or public policy. It is manifestly contrary to
the public interest that unlawful bargains or transactions should be accepted
as being of equal status and value as those which are lawful; or that such arrangements
should be accorded recognition in and by courts that determine and apply the
law;
or that a party who has voluntarily engaged in some form of illegality
should be permitted to seek the protection and aid of those courts in the event
that the transaction is not performed as originally intended, with the result
that he is out of pocket and the other party has derived some monetary
advantage at his expense.  In such circumstances the policy of the law is that
the loss should lie where it falls.  It would be improper, and contradictory to
the nature and functions of courts, to allow their jurisdiction to be invoked
.
[emphasis added; footnotes omitted]

[
46
]

The test for establishing that a statement of
claim discloses no reasonable claim is that set out by Wilson J. in
Hunt
v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, 74 D.L.R. (4th) 321 [cited
to S.C.R.] at 980:

Thus, the test in
Canada governing the application of provisions like Rule 19(24)(a) of the
British Columbia
Rules of Court
is the same as the one that
governs an application under R.S.C. O. 18, r. 19: assuming that the facts as
stated in the statement of claim can be proved, is it "plain and
obvious" that the plaintiff's statement of claim discloses no reasonable
cause of action? As in England, if there is a chance that the plaintiff might
succeed, then the plaintiff should not be "driven from the judgment
seat". Neither the length and complexity of the issues, the novelty of the
cause of action, nor the potential for the defendant to present a strong defence
should prevent the plaintiff from proceeding with his or her case. Only if the
action is certain to fail because it contains a radical defect ranking with the
others listed in Rule 19(24) of the British Columbia
Rules of Court

should the relevant portions of a plaintiff's statement of claim be struck out
under Rule 19(24)(a).

[
47
]

The case law cited by RBC is authority for the
propositions that:

(a)       the proceeds of fraud are held by
recpients subject to a constructive trust in favour of a victim of the fraud
and subject to tracing claims.  This is so whether the recipient is the
perpetrator of the fraud or received the proceeds as a volunteer.  An exception
to this rule applies to those who receive the proceeds as part of a bona fide
transaction, for value, without notice of the trust, see
ICBC v. Lo

2006 BCCA 584
, 63 B.C.L.R. (4th) 71,
ICBC
v. Dragon

Driving School

2007 BCSC 389
, 156 A.C.W.S. (3d)
456,
British Columbia Teachers Credit Union v. Betterly
(1975),

1975 CanLII 1032 (BC SC)
, 61 DLR (3d) 755;

(b)       a right to demand payment of funds on
account with one’s banker is a claim in debt; it is a chose in action and,
therefore, property over which a trust may be imposed.  Similarly, a judgment
which entitles one to enforce or recover damages against ones’ bank for
refusing to honour a demand for payment of funds on account is property that
may be subject to a constructive trust; see
Citadel General Assurance Co.
v. Lloyds Bank Canada
,
1997 CanLII 334 (SCC)
, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 805, 152 D.L.R. (4th) 411;]

(c)        a party may be liable for knowing
receipt of trust funds where:

(a)       the party receives trust property for their own use and
benefit; and

(b)       the party has knowledge of the breach of trust; actual
knowledge, wilful blindness, recklessness, or constructive knowledge will
suffice;

(d)       a party
will be found to have constructive knowledge of a breach of trust where they
are aware of suspicious circumstances which put the recipient on notice that
they may be receiving the funds in breach of trust and the party receiving the
funds fails to make adequate inquiry.

[
48
]

In my view, the defendants’ arguments go to the
merits of RBC’s claim.  However, these submissions do not establish that it is
plain and obvious that the action is certain to fail.  RBC has pleaded the
facts necessary to support a cause of action for damages, equitable relief for
breach of trust, knowing receipt and to assert proprietary and tracing claims
with respect to the Disputed Property.  It is not for the Court in the context
of the present application to delve further into an evaluation of the prospects
for success of the action.

[
49
]

In the result, the defendants have not
established that the action should be struck pursuant to rule 19(24)(a) as
disclosing no reasonable claim.

[
50
]

Counsel for the defendants conceded that the
defendant’s application for summary judgment pursuant to rule 18(6) is to be
determined on the same basis.  Accordingly, the defendants have failed to
establish that there is no merit in the plaintiffs claim and the application
pursuant to rule 18(6) is dismissed.

19(24)(b) Scandalous, Frivolous, Vexatious

[
51
]

The defendants submit that the claim should be
struck pursuant to rule 19(24)(b).  They submit that the matters raised with
respect to the conduct of RBC that were addressed with respect to rule
19(24)(a) are relevant to the considerations under this sub-section as well.
They submit in addition that RBC has persisted with allegations known to be
untrue, that it is attempting to re-litigate matters already determined.  The defendants
have many complaints with respect to the conduct of RBC in the litigation,
generally to the effect that RBC is seeking to add the costs, stress and
economic burdens of the litigation with procedural steps it has taken.

[
52
]

In
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266, 91 A.C.W.S. (3d)
(B.C.S.C.), Romilly J. discussed the requirements for the application of rule
19(24)(b) at paras 46-47:

The authorities provide little guidance as to
what constitutes pleadings that are “unnecessary”, “scandalous”, “frivolous” or
“embarrassing”. However some principles do emerge.

Irrelevancy and
embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it is
difficult to understand what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco
Audio-Publishers Inc
.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C.S.C.). An
“embarrassing” and “scandalous” pleading is one that is so irrelevant that it
will involve the parties in useless expense and will prejudice the trial of the
action by involving them in a dispute apart from the issues:
Keddie v.
Dumas Hotels Ltd.
(
Cariboo Trail Hotel
) (1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62
B.C.L.R. 145 (B.C.C.A) at 147. An allegation which is scandalous will not be
struck if it is relevant to the proceedings. It will only be struck if
irrelevant as well as scandalous:
College of Dental Surgeons of British Columbia
v. Cleland
(1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
, 66 W.W.R. 499 (B.C.C.A.). A pleading is
“unnecessary” or “vexatious” if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff’s
cause of action or does not advance any claim known in law:
Strauts v.
Harrigan
, (December 2, 1991), Doc. Vancouver C913631 (B.C.S.C.). A
pleading that is superfluous will not be struck out if it is not necessarily
unnecessary or otherwise objectionable:
Lutz v. Canadian Puget Sound
Lumber and Timber Co.

(1920), 28 B.C.R. 39 (C.A.)
. A pleading is
“frivolous” if it is obviously unsustainable, not in the sense that it lacks an
evidentiary basis, but because of the doctrine of estoppel:
Chrisgian v.
B.C. Rail Ltd. et al.
, (July 3, 1992), Doc. Prince George 20714 (B.C.
Master).

[
53
]

The RBC pleadings do not meet the test for
matters which are unnecessary, scandalous or frivolous.  The pleadings disclose
a cause of action.  The allegations in the pleadings advance the causes of
action that are raised.

[
54
]

In
Ebrahim v. Ebrahim
,
2002 BCSC
466
, aff’d
2003 BCCA 94
, Madam Justice Gill provided the following explanation
of the term vexatious in relation to rule 19(24) at para. 15:

In
Law Society of Upper Canada v. Chavali

(1998), 21 C.P.C. (4th) 20 (Ont. Gen. Div.)
aff'd
(1998), 31 C.P.C. (4th) 221
(Ont. C.A.)
, Cummings J., considered the meaning of vexatious. He stated, at 20-21:

The adjective
"vexatious" is defined by the
Concise Oxford Dictionary
, 9th
ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1995) as:

1.         such as to
cause vexation.

2.         Law not
having sufficient grounds for action and seeking only to annoy the defendant.

To "vex" is
defined as "to anger by a slight or a petty annoyance; irritate".

In
Lang Michener
Lash Johnston v. Fabian
(1987),
1987 CanLII 172 (ON HCJ)
, 59 O.R. (2d) 353 (Ont. H.C.), the
Honourable Mr. Justice Henry summarized the salient charcteristics and
principles relating to vexatious proceedings and conduct as follows (at
358-359):

(a)        the
bringing of one or more actions to determine an issue which has already been
determined by a court of competent jurisdiction constitutes a vexatious
proceeding;

(b)       where it is
obvious that an action cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no
possible good, or if no reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain
relief, the action is vexatious;

(c)        vexatious
actions include those brought for an improper purpose, including the harassment
and oppression of other parties by multifarious proceedings brought for
purposes other than the assertion of legitimate rights;

(d)       it is a
general characteristic of vexatious proceedings that grounds and issues raised
tend to be rolled forward into subsequent actions and repeated and
supplemented, often with actions  brought against the lawyers who have acted
for or against the litigant in earlier proceedings;

(e)       in
determining whether proceedings are vexatious, the court must look at the whole
history of the matter and not just whether there was originally a good cause of
action;

(f)         the
failure of the person instituting the proceedings to pay the costs of
unsuccessful proceedings is one factor to be considered in determining whether
proceedings are vexatious;

(g)       the
respondent's conduct in persistently taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial
decisions can be considered vexatious conduct of legal proceedings.

The matter of "vexatious" must be
determined by an objective standard. See, for example:
Mascan Corp. v.
French
(1988),
1988 CanLII 4731 (ON CA)
, 64 O.R. (2d) 1 (C.A.) at 7;
Children's Aid Society
of Ottawa-Carleton v. M.B.
,
[1997] O.J. No. 1964
(Ont. Ct. (Gen. Div.))
at para. 22.

[
55
]

The question of whether this litigation concerns
a matter that has already been determined is a variant of the submission that
the action constitutes a collateral attack upon or an attempt to re-litigate
the BNS Action and will be addressed in relation to the submissions concerning
rule 19(24)(d).  Leaving that issue to one side, it is not obvious that the
action as constituted cannot succeed or that RBC could not have a reasonable
expectation that it could obtain relief.  There is in my view no evidence that
this action has been brought for an improper purpose.  While the defendants
have many complaints about the conduct of the litigation, I have seen no
evidence of impropriety.  There is no history of RBC rolling matters forward or
taking unsuccessful appeal.  Indeed, RBC was not a party to the BNS Action.

[
56
]

The defendants have not established that the
claim by RBC is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious pursuant to rule
19(24)(b).

Rule 19(24)(d) Abuse of Process

[
57
]

The defendants submit that the essence of the
BNS Action was the determination of who owned or was entitled to the Funds.
Moreover, at all times BNS, having itself no interest in the Funds, was acting
as the proxy of RBC.  Throughout the BNS Action, BNS asserted the equitable
principles relevant to RBC interest in the Funds to justify and defend its
conduct.  Accordingly, the defendants submit RBC Action is precluded by the
doctrines of
res judicata
and collateral attack and the claim should be
struck pursuant to rule 18(24)(d).

[
58
]

The defendants submit further that RBC, having a
sufficient interest in the BNS Action, and having chosen not to intervene, is
bound by the results of that action.  The defendants cite
Banque Nationale
de Paris (Canada) v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce
(2001),
2001 CanLII 24099 (ON CA)
, 195
D.L.R. (4th) 308, 52 O.R. (3d) 161 (C.A.).

[
59
]

The two main branches of
res judicata

were described by Dickson J., as he then was, in
Angle v. M.N.R.
,

1974 CanLII 168 (SCC)
, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 248, 47 D.L.R. (3d) 544 [
Angle
cited to S.C.R.]
at 254 as follows:

The first ‘cause of action estoppel’, precludes
a person from bringing an action against another when that same cause of action
has been determined in earlier proceedings by a court of competent
jurisdiction... The second species of estoppel
per rem judicatam
is
known as “issue estoppel”...

Lord Guest in
Carl Zeiss Stiftung v. Rayner
& Keeler Ltd. (No. 2)
, at p. 935, defined the requirements of issue
estoppel as:

... (1) that the same question has been
decided; (2) that the judicial decision which is said to create the estoppel
was final; and, (3) that the parties to the judicial decision or their privies
were the same persons as the parties to the proceedings in which the estoppel
is raised or their privies ..... [footnotes omitted]

[
60
]

It is clear that the BNS Action resulted in a
final judicial decision.  It is also not disputed by RBC that, for purposes of
consideration of those issues, RBC was a privy of BNS.  The question is whether
the same question or cause of action that was determined in the BNS Action is
alleged in the present action.  In my view, neither the causes of action nor
the questions are the same and, accordingly, the present action is not barred
by the doctrine of
res judicata
.

[
61
]

The BNS Action was a claim in which the
plaintiffs (defendants in this action) asserted that BNS had breached its
contractual and statutory obligations.  In the result, BNS was found to have
been in breach of its obligations and was ordered to pay damages.  It is the
case that the equities of RBC that are the subject of the present action were
raised by BNS and considered by the court in the BNS Action.  That was, however,
in the context of determining whether those equities created a defence for BNS
to the plaintiffs’ claims.  In my view, the Court in the BNS appeal was not
adjudicating the “ownership of the Funds” as the defendants in the present case
now characterize it, nor was it addressing the equities as between RBC and the
defendants.

[
62
]

In my view, circumstances in the case at bar are
similar to those in
Angle
.  The facts of that case as set out in
the headnote were:

Appellant, president and controlling shareholder
of Transworld Explorations Limited, caused the company to construct a pool
house, with furniture and fixtures, at the rear of her property. Six months
after the foundations were in, appellant purported to lease to the company the
whole of her property for five years at one dollar per year. After construction
was complete, appellant leased the property to the company by a second lease
for one year, at a rental of $6,000 payable in monthly instalments of $500. In
order to create the impression that the pool house had been paid for, the
husband of appellant arranged a bank loan of $50,000 to appellant. This sum was
deposited to the credit of the company, which could not withdraw it until the
loan was paid. The husband then gave the appellant a cheque drawn on the
company's account and signed by him as agent for the company in order that she
could repay the bank loan, which she did.

Appellant was assessed under s. 8(1)(c) of the
Income
Tax Act
, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, $52,243.58 for benefits from construction
of the pool house, and $5,995.82 for furniture and fixtures. On appeal the
Exchequer Court concluded that appellant had received the house as owner of the
freehold and that the procedure employed by appellant did not constitute
payment for the house, and it affirmed the assessment except for the furniture
and fixtures.

Some time after these
proceedings the Minister of National Revenue, in an effort to collect arrears
of taxes from another company, obtained
ex parte
an order for a writ of
extent in the second degree, against Transworld as debtor of the other company;
a writ of extent in the third degree was also issued against appellant as
debtor of Transworld. Other writs of extent were also issued, but set aside
following a motion to set aside; however, the writ issued against appellant was
upheld. The latter appealed this decision, on the ground that the judgment of
the Exchequer Court rendered the matter of appellant's alleged indebtedness
res
judicata
.

[
63
]

Mr. Justice Dickson, for the majority, described
the requirements for the matters to be the same question at 254-255:

Is the question to be decided in these
proceedings, namely the indebtedness of Mrs. Angle to Transworld Explorations
Limited, the same as was contested in the earlier proceedings? If it is not,
there is no estoppel. It will not suffice if the question arose collaterally or
incidentally in the earlier proceedings or is one which must be inferred by
argument from the judgment. That is plain from the words of De Grey C.J.
in the
Duchess of Kingston's

case
[(1776), 20 St.
Tr. 355, 538n.], quoted by Lord Selborne L.J. in
R. v. Hutchings

[
(1881), 6 Q.B.D. 300
.], at p. 304, and by Lord Radcliffe in
Society of
Medical Officers of Health v. Hope
[
[1960] A.C. 551
.]. The question out
of which the estoppel is said to arise must have been "fundamental to the
decision arrived at" in the earlier proceedings:
per
Lord Shaw

in

Hoystead v. Commissioner of Taxation
[
1925 CanLII 607 (UK JCPC)
, [1926] A.C. 155.]. The
authors of Spencer Bower and Turner,
Doctrine of Res Judicata
, 2nd ed.
pp. 181, 182, quoted by Megarry J. in
Spens v. I.R.C.
[
[1970] 3
All. E.R. 295
.], at p. 301, set forth in these words the nature of the enquiry
which must be made:

... whether the
determination on which it is sought to found the estoppel is "so fundamental"
to the substantive decision that the latter
cannot stand
without the
former. Nothing less than this will do.

And further at 247:

As long ago as 1893, Lord Hobhouse said in the
Privy Council in
Attorney General for Trinidad and Tobago v. Eriché

[
[1893] A.C. 518
.], at p. 522:

It is hardly necessary
to refer at length to authorities for the elementary principle that in order to
establish the plea of res judicata the judgment relied on must have been
pronounced by a Court having concurrent or exclusive jurisdiction directly upon
the point. In the
Duchess of Kingston's Case
, Sm. L.C. vol. ii.
p. 642, which is constantly referred to for the law on this subject, it is laid
down that in order to establish the plea of res judicata the Court whose
judgment is invoked must have had jurisdiction and have given judgment directly
upon the matter in question; but that if the matter came collaterally into
question in the first Court, or were only incidentally cognizable by it, or
merely to be inferred by argument from the judgment, the judgment is not
conclusive.

The question not
being
eadem questio
, I am of the opinion that this is not a case for
application of the principle of issue estoppel.

[
64
]

In the case at bar, while the issue of RBC’s
equities came collaterally into question, in my view, the Court of Appeal did
not give judgment on that matter.

[
65
]

The doctrine of collateral attack is a separate,
but related doctrine.  This doctrine was described in
Chapman v. Canada
(Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs)
,
2003 BCCA 665
, 21 B.C.L.R.
(4th) 272, by Madam Justice Saunders, speaking for the court at para. 20 as
follows:

Separate from the notion of
res judicata
,
but related in the sense that it also is encompassed by the term abuse of
process, is the rule against collateral attack described by McIntyre J. in
R.
v. Wilson
,
1983 CanLII 35 (SCC)
, [1983] 2 S.C.R. 594, (S.C.C.) at 599, also cited by the
chambers judge:

It has long been a fundamental rule that a
court order, made by a court having jurisdiction to make it, stands and is
binding and conclusive unless it is set aside on appeal or lawfully quashed. It
is also well settled in the authorities that such an order may not be attacked
collaterally and a collateral attack may be described as an attack made in
proceedings other than those whose specific object is the reversal, variation,
or nullification of the order or judgment. Where appeals have been exhausted
and other means of direct attack upon a judgment or order, such as proceedings
by prerogative writs or proceedings for judicial review, have been unavailing,
the only recourse open to one who seeks to set aside a court order is an action
for review in the High Court where grounds for such a proceeding exist. Without
attempting a complete list, such grounds would include fraud or the discovery
of new evidence.

[
66
]

The question with respect to the doctrine of
collateral attack is therefore whether RBC seeks in the present action to
reverse, vary or nullify the judgment in the BNS Action.  In my view, the RBC Action
does not seek to do so and does not constitute a collateral attack on the BNS
judgment.  The judgment in the BNS Action was that BNS was in breach of
obligations it owed to the plaintiffs in that action and as a consequence, it
was ordered to pay damages to the plaintiffs.  What the defendants are
asserting in the present application is that if RBC succeeds in this action, the
defendants will not be able to keep the proceeds of the BNS litigation but will
be forced to give them over to RBC.  However, RBC is no different from any
other creditor in that circumstance.  Because the BNS Action did not determine
entitlement to the Funds as between RBC and the defendants, the present action
is not an attempt to vary, nullify or reverse the BNS Action.

[
67
]

Finally, the defendants contend that the claim
should be struck as an abuse of process because RBC did not take steps to have
this action heard at the same time as the BNS action.

[
68
]

Counsel for BNS, who was at the time also
counsel for RBC, raised the issue that the matters should be heard together in
advance of the rule 18A application.  Counsel for the BNS plaintiffs in the BNS
Action, wanting to proceed with the 18A application, objected.  Then, after the
first Court of Appeal decision in the BNS Action, counsel for the banks sought
the plaintiffs’ consent to have the matters heard together.  Counsel objected
and the matter was not pursued further.

[
69
]

An action is to be struck pursuant to rule
19(24) only in clear cases.  In my view, with the benefit of hindsight, one can
say that the matters should have been heard together.  It would certainly have
been a more efficient use of the court’s time.  However, at the time each
party, for their own reasons, reasons that on the materials before me appeared
to be not unreasonable, decided to proceed with the BNS Action first.  I am not
prepared in these circumstances to say that it is an abuse of process for RBC
to proceed.

[
70
]

Accordingly, the defendants’ application is
dismissed.

“Ross
J.”
